species.name: Pelidnota punctata
species.intro: For grapevine beetles I would set out two foods before introducing a pair. Adults feed mainly on the leaves of wild and cultivated grapes. The moment a grub hatches, it can bore into soft, decaying hardwood. William P. Hayes followed both stages in Kansas and recorded which hardwood carried a brood all the way to adulthood.

sections.title: Adult food and pairing
sections.text: I recommend fresh grape foliage for the adults. They also eat the grapes themselves and sometimes feed on Virginia creeper. During the day the beetles often rest on their host plants. After dark they take flight, sometimes coming to lights, and pairs meet on the vines. Evening is a good time to watch the foliage for mating. Hayes also saw a captive pair mate on the soil during the afternoon.

sections.title: The laying site and eggs
sections.text: For the laying site I would put moist soil directly against soft, decomposed hardwood. Females place eggs singly in the soil under a log or beside a rotten stump, sometimes enclosing each egg in a small ball of earth. Kansas laying records ran from June 19 to August 17. A fresh egg is pearly white and oval, about 2.0 by 1.5 mm. It expands and rounds out before hatching. Incubation spanned 8–26 days in the laboratory and averaged about 15 days.

sections.title: Feeding the grubs
sections.text: Rotten elm is my first choice when following Hayes’s method. Hayes placed hatchlings together in a large container of crumbled, decaying elm in July 1920 and left them undisturbed. When he examined the container two years later, it held 12 recently matured males and 17 females. In the wild, grubs also tunnel into the decayed roots of stumps. Walnut, cherry and birch are among the other hardwoods recorded. Larvae overwinter in the wood, and individuals can reach their third instar either before their first winter or the following year.

sections.title: Pupation and the next adults
sections.text: I would allow about two full years from egg laying before expecting new adults. The inactive prepupal period lasted 3–9 days in Kansas. In a series of 21 pupae, the pupal stage lasted 13–24 days and averaged 19. One beetle tracked individually from an egg laid in early July 1919 became an adult on July 11, 1921, closely matching the two-year interval in the elm container.

species.name: Odontotaenius disjunctus
species.intro: A horned passalus family uses the same piece of decaying hardwood as a nest and a food supply. Both parents cut galleries, prepare food for the grubs and tend the brood through pupation. A section of occupied wood may therefore contain a breeding pair, larvae of several sizes and newly emerged adults together. For this species, I would start with a family and its occupied wood.

sections.title: Housing a family
sections.text: I would choose moist, well-decayed hardwood that still holds together well enough for tunnels. University of Florida keepers recommend using the rotted oak in which the beetles were found. Preserve the occupied galleries when moving a family, and add more softened wood as the adults consume it. Keep established broods together. In an experiment by King and Fashing, larval mortality was higher with adults that had never reproduced than with the larvae’s own parents or with unrelated adults already caring for young.

sections.title: Eggs and larval food
sections.text:
Pairs mate inside the log. An early field account recorded about 20–35 eggs per pair over May and June, which explains why a single gallery can contain larvae of quite different ages. Clusters of eggs lie among the adults’ frass, and the parents can pick them up with their mandibles and move them within the nest. Individual eggs enlarge from about 3.0 × 2.4 mm at laying to 3.7 × 3.2 mm shortly before hatching.
I would leave the fine material along the gallery walls in place. The grubs eat wood their parents have chewed, together with frass. A resting grub curls into a C. Its first two pairs of legs are conspicuous, while the hind pair is so reduced that the animal can appear to have only four legs.

sections.title: Pupal chambers and young adults
sections.text: Adults enclose the developing pupae in chambers made with wood particles and other debris. They repair breaks in the chamber, and older siblings can help do this even while their own adult cuticle is still hardening. I would leave an intact chamber with the family, even if a young adult is sharing that section of the gallery. Newly emerged beetles are reddish and gradually darken to black. Depending on moisture and temperature, the life cycle can fit within a summer or extend to 14–16 months. Some pupae overwinter in the log.

species.name: Tenebrio molitor
species.intro: The yellow mealworm is the larval stage of a darkling beetle. Wheat bran can carry a colony through its entire life cycle. The adults lay in it, the hatchlings feed where they emerge, and mature larvae can be set aside to produce the next generation of beetles. For a small culture, I recommend dating each laying tray so the broods are easy to follow.

sections.title: Preparing a breeding tray
sections.text: For the adults I would use a shallow, ventilated tray of dry wheat bran with small pieces of carrot for moisture. Give only as much carrot as the beetles will use before it spoils. A published wheat-bran colony at the University of Thessaly used fine mesh on the lid and fresh potato slices twice a week. Its beetles bred at 26 °C and 50% relative humidity in darkness. The researchers transferred the adults to fresh bran each week and left the eggs in the original tray. The laying interval gives a useful estimate of the ages of the young that appear later.

sections.title: Eggs and growing larvae
sections.text:
The females burrow and often deposit eggs near the tray floor. Retain the used grain even if it looks empty. For a large colony, a screen with openings around 2 mm wide lets females lay through it while keeping the adults away from the eggs. Adults can otherwise eat eggs in crowded trays.
A Norwegian trial used about 500 adults in each 53.5 × 34.5 × 5.6 cm tray. Each group had 400 g of wheat bran or milled oat by-product for two weeks of laying. After removing the adults, the researchers added 600 g of the same feed and provided carrots for moisture. Both feeds supported larvae through the ten-week sampling age. The researchers kept the wheat-bran group longer to obtain pupae and adults.

sections.title: Keeping the next generation
sections.text: To keep the colony going, I would set aside some large larvae to mature. Pupation can extend across several weeks in one tray. Pick out the pale pupae as they appear because feeding larvae can injure or eat them. Lay them in a single layer on a little bran. Inagro’s rearing guide reports adult emergence after about seven to eight days under its production conditions. Move the new beetles into a breeding tray with fresh bran and a moisture source to begin another dated batch.

species.name: Gymnetis thula
species.intro: For a colony of harlequin flower beetles, I plan for two appetites. The day-flying adults gather around ripe fruit at the surface. Beneath them, females lay in decomposing plant material, and the young grubs start feeding as soon as they hatch.

sections.title: Feeding and watching the adults
sections.text: I recommend starting with soft banana or apple, both favorites in the Roach Crossing colony. Rosamond Gifford Zoo also feeds its beetles ripe fruit and vegetable scraps. Outdoors, adults visit flowers and feed at sap flows, including those of false willow in Texas. They are quick to take wing if disturbed, so use a covered enclosure and check the underside of the lid as you lift it. Captive adults have lived as long as eight months. A colony may still have actively feeding adults well after its first larvae appear.

sections.title: Preparing the breeding substrate
sections.text: Prepare a loose bed of decayed plant matter below the fruit. Females lay in compost or fermenting oak, and larvae will eat the material surrounding the eggs. In the wild, grubs occupy decomposed material in tree cavities, including hollows in post oak and mesquite. In culture, rotting wood and compost make good starting materials. The Roach Crossing colony also consumed decomposing yard vegetation. Aim for a moist mixture loose enough for the larvae to move through. Check below the surface when judging moisture, especially in a shallow enclosure.

sections.title: Recognizing pupation
sections.text: The white, curved grubs grow through three instars and can reach about 25 mm. When replacing old substrate, check for oval cells before breaking up the lumps. These larvae can build chambers from their own frass, so what looks like spent substrate can contain a pupa. Leave each occupied cell in place. In the Roach Crossing colony, adults emerged several weeks after pupating. Once the beetles appear at the surface, offer fresh fruit again. The amount of cream on the head, thorax and wing covers varies from one adult to the next.

species.name: Dynastes tityus
species.intro: I have raised hundreds of eastern Hercules beetles in Michigan. I can rear a large brood on organic raised-bed soil, and I have also raised sizeable males on used substrate. A newly formed adult may sit through the winter in its pupal chamber, so I plan the next pairing around when the beetles actually come up and feed.

sections.title: Feeding and pairing active adults
sections.text:
I keep an active male and female together. I offer beetle jelly every five days, or a piece of apple or banana. I watch for the female to feed and burrow before checking for eggs. I prefer to see a mating when I can. In my experience, roughly a third of the wild-caught females I have worked with appeared to be unmated. A female from the Texas Sandhills was one of them.
Season matters when putting a pair together. Adults I collected in northern Florida in 2024 became active in late May the following year. I wait for both beetles to be active before pairing them.

sections.title: Choosing substrate for a large brood
sections.text:
When I was raising hundreds at once, I used a locally available organic raised-bed soil as a cheaper alternative to flake soil. It worked for my Michigan colony, although I had to change it more often. Products sold as raised-bed soil vary from place to place. Before using a whole bag for a brood, I would try a small batch and follow how well the grubs feed and grow. The major males I raised this way measured about 55–62 mm. I never reached 65 mm with that method.
I have also obtained males over 55 mm on spent substrate that the larvae had reduced almost entirely to dry frass. That was a separate trial. For a new brood I would start with fresh larval food and replace it as the grubs consume it.

sections.title: Wood in the field and in culture
sections.text: Tree cavities are a good place to look for the loose material the larvae eat. I have seen this species use standing dead pine. In 2021 I received Alabama beetles from Alan that had been found in pine and raised on potting soil. I keep that distinction in mind when choosing a substrate. The material a grub came from in the woods and the food it developed on afterward can be quite different.

sections.title: Pupal chambers and overwintering
sections.text: Once a grub finishes shaping its chamber, I leave it intact. Alan found wild adults still inside their chambers on three separate occasions, in October, November and April. He gives about two to three years for larval development in the wild. Inside a clear container, I can follow a chamber at the wall without opening it. I begin offering food once the adult leaves the chamber and comes to the surface.

species.name: Lucanus elaphus
species.intro: I started my giant stag beetle line with wild adults from North Carolina. By fall I had a brood of larvae, and I raised them to adulthood. To get that captive-bred generation reproducing, I gave the adults a long, cool rest. Their eggs hatched, and I now have second-generation grubs from the original North Carolina beetles.

sections.title: Setting up a laying female
sections.text: I recommend a shoebox-sized container of flake soil and pieces of decaying hardwood. The Mantis Menagerie used one such box for each of four wild females that had flown to a light shortly after sunset. A few months later those females had produced dozens of larvae. Offer active adults ripe fruit for its sugary juice. Leave the wood embedded in the bedding while a female is laying. When you lift a piece, check the fine material against its sides and underside. Benjamin Harink has described eggs in precisely that position.

sections.title: Feeding the grubs
sections.text: Use white-rotted hardwood or a fermented wood substrate. A measured alternative comes from Ulyshen and colleagues, who found wild larvae feeding inside damp Mississippi logs and underneath them at the soil surface. For each grub they filled a ventilated container with about 500 mL of an equal-parts mix of slightly decayed oak chips and thoroughly decayed, crumbly oak. Add enough water that a squeezed handful releases some moisture and the mix holds its water when left alone. The team kept these containers at 21–23 °C.

sections.title: Watching for pupation
sections.text: Check the underside of the container before opening it. Most grubs in the Mississippi study built their chambers against the bottom, where the pupal molt could be seen through the wall. Among beetles that pupated within a year of collection, females averaged about 29 days as pupae and males 31. Sixteen males stayed larvae for an extra year. Alan waited several months for prepupae in his culture. His stalled grubs entered that stage together after a faulty air conditioner cooled the room for several days in July. Allow one to two years for development and give slower individuals time.

sections.title: Overwintering my adults
sections.text: I kept my captive-bred adults in a wine cooler for eight months at about 55 °F (13 °C). They laid eggs over the next two months, roughly ten months after reaching adulthood. Seeing those eggs hatch is why I recommend repeating that cool rest with this North Carolina line.

species.name: Chrysina woodi
species.intro: The first thing I notice about a live Chrysina woodi is the contrast between its emerald-green back and its metallic blue feet. I bred this scarab from West Texas adults. A pair needs fresh foliage throughout the laying period, and a mature grub needs a place to build its pupal cell below its food.

facts.title: Larval period
facts.text: 1.5–3 years in the seasonally cooled culture. My West Texas stock reached adulthood in about six months.

facts.title: Egg count
facts.text: 20–60 or more in the seasonal culture. One West Texas female laid 122 eggs.

sections.title: Choosing and feeding the adults
sections.text: I start with fresh hickory foliage. My West Texas adults fed on it readily. Alan uses walnut or hickory and recommends pecan as an alternative in the eastern United States. He keeps spare cuttings in a closed bag in the refrigerator for about a week and gives the beetles fresh branches every three days. Outdoors, adults fly along mountain arroyos on cloudy days and at night, particularly in humid summer weather. To sex a pair, look underneath the tip of the abdomen. Alan distinguishes females by a fine line down the middle of the terminal segment. Males have a dark segment that is absent in females. Adults measure about 25–35 mm.

sections.title: Setting up a laying enclosure
sections.text: I favor a well-ventilated enclosure and the lightly fermented flake soil used for stag beetles. Alan recommends a medium-size ventilated Critter Keeper or larger, with at least 1.75 US gallons (6.6 L) of enclosure capacity. Add 3 inches (7.5 cm) of loose flake soil. Leave it uncompacted, with just enough water that a handful holds together when squeezed and releases no drops. Females may spend several days feeding, disappear into the substrate to lay, then return to the branches. He leaves the eggs in place to hatch because his adults leave them unharmed. Alan gives an egg count of 20–60 or more and an adult lifespan of one to three months. He rates this species 8 out of 10 for breeding difficulty.

sections.title: Larval food, winter cooling and pupation
sections.text: I recommend raising the grubs individually. Flake soil and decayed wood both serve as larval food. In fall, Alan places about 2 inches (5 cm) of clay or similarly textured pupation soil beneath the feeding layer once the grubs reach the late third instar. He keeps them through winter from the low 40s into the 50s °F (roughly 5–15 °C), then warms them in spring. Without cooling, some grubs failed to pupate and some adults emerged too far apart to pair. After spring warming, adults come to the surface on their own over the next few months. Alan lets newly surfaced females feed away from males for several days before pairing them. He gives 1½–3 years for the larval stage in his culture and about a month as a pupa. My West Texas stock developed much faster.

species.name: Xyloryctes thestalus
species.intro: After three years of trying to breed the western rhinoceros beetle, I finally reared adults from eggs laid in captivity. The surprise was the timing. My adults produced just one egg before winter. Most of the breeding happened the following spring, after beetles that had spent months underground returned to the surface and began feeding again.

sections.title: Setting up and feeding the adults
sections.text: I used a well-ventilated enclosure with 4–5 in (10–13 cm) of lightly fermented flake soil and pieces of bark across the surface. I kept the flake soil slightly moist, around the moisture level I use for stag beetles and a little drier than I ordinarily use for rhinoceros beetles. The adults showed a clear preference for apple and other firm fruits over softer foods.

sections.title: Overwintering and spring egg laying
sections.text:
By late October the adults had buried themselves and stopped eating. I kept the enclosure at about 68–75 °F (20–24 °C) throughout the winter. They stayed below the surface until April. When they came back up, they fed again and breeding activity increased. The single egg laid before winter eventually produced a male. All the other eggs and larvae I recovered came from April through July. On June 30, 2023, I found both fresh eggs and young grubs in the enclosure of my Fort Davis, Texas stock.
I would keep an apparently unproductive autumn setup through the following spring. Some of the wild adults I collected on August 5, 2022, were still alive more than a year later. Their ability to resume feeding and breeding after such a long interval underground made it worth keeping the colony together.

sections.title: Burrowing and larval food in the wild
sections.text: Morón and Zaragoza observed adults near Villa de Allende, Mexico, excavating individual daytime retreats in soft soil, both in the field and in captivity. The galleries reached 20–25 cm below the surface. In the same area they found third-instar larvae 10–20 cm beneath oak leaf litter, feeding on the older, decomposing leaves. This field record documents a larval food alongside the lightly fermented flake soil used in my breeding enclosure.

species.name: Strategus aloeus
species.intro: One of the males I bred measured 53 mm. For such a substantial beetle, the ox beetle has a surprisingly short larval period and a long adult life. My larvae reached adulthood in less than a year on organic raised-bed soil. Once the adults were active, keeping up with their appetite took more attention than preparing the breeding substrate.

sections.title: Adult care and laying
sections.text: My adults ate heavily, so I supplied fresh food every three days. Beetle jelly, apple and banana are my usual choices for fruit-feeding adults. Adult males can live as long as two years. The longest-lived female in my own colony survived about nine months. My females accepted several organic substrates for laying, so I was able to use a simple setup. In July, Alan photographed the eggs of a wild-caught female through the clear wall of her enclosure. One male I had photographed as a pupa in January 2022 was still alive and well the following January.

sections.title: Rearing the grubs and providing a pupal cell
sections.text: Organic raised-bed soil carried my grubs through to adulthood. Alan also documented captive-bred larvae feeding in flake soil, a fermented sawdust substrate. Those series offer two practical starting points. As the grubs approach pupation, I like to provide a layer of very firmly packed topsoil where they can construct their chambers. I have also had adults develop without that layer. The photograph of my pupa and Alan’s photographs of male and female pupae show the stage between the feeding grub and the heavily built adult.

sections.title: Developmental timing in a published colony
sections.text: Ahumada and colleagues measured each stage in beetles from Puerto Wilches, Colombia, reared at 29–32 °C. Eggs averaged about 15 days to hatch. Of the three larval instars, the first averaged 24 days, the second 42 days and the third about 201 days. Pupation averaged another 27 days, bringing the egg-to-adult interval to about 308 days. That long final instar accounts for much of the wait after a grub has become conspicuously large. For comparison, my own larvae completed development in raised-bed soil in less than a year.

sections.title: Keeping eastern and western stocks separate
sections.text: I keep locality labels with each line and pair beetles from the same regional stock. I treat the eastern and western populations as two putative species within the Strategus aloeus complex. I group Arizona and New Mexico with the western stock, and western Texas eastward with the eastern stock. I cannot assign my 2022 captive series to either group from its locality data.

species.name: Mallodon dasystomus
species.intro: A large hardwood stump borer can approach 5 cm in length. I consider it a good first longhorn to rear because the females accept a simple bed of damp sawdust and the larvae feed on hardwood pellets after they have been expanded into sawdust. The main commitment is time. The larvae can spend several years feeding before they mature.

sections.title: Pairing adults
sections.text: Adults are nocturnal, and their behavior is easiest to interpret once the two beetles have made contact. In laboratory pairings observed under red light, a male first touched the female with his antennae, paused, turned his body into line with hers, mounted and curled his abdomen beneath hers. Fifteen of 17 males showed this complete sequence. The other encounters included indifference or aggression, and males sometimes bit a female’s legs or wing covers. When I introduce a pair, I stay close enough to separate them if one starts biting the other.

sections.title: Egg laying and egg recognition
sections.text: In the field, females lay where hardwood is exposed, often at a wound near the base of a stressed tree. In my setup, about half an inch (1.3 cm) of damp sawdust was sufficient for laying. I could check that shallow layer for eggs without taking a log apart. The eggs have a hard shell and can look surprisingly like seeds among the wood particles. The half-inch measurement applies to the female’s laying container.

sections.title: Larval food and development
sections.text:
I reared the larvae on plain hardwood sawdust from expanded pellets. They also accept kinshi, a block of sawdust colonized by fungal mycelium. In my experience the larvae took supplementary protein and could grow quickly when it was available. I allow about one to three years for the larval stage, depending on the rearing conditions.
Field records give a useful comparison. Young larvae feed beneath the bark before boring through the sapwood and into the heartwood. Recorded hosts include oak, hickory, sweetgum, sugarberry and willow. Development in a tree commonly takes three to four years. The emerging adult leaves a large oval hole in the wood.

species.name: Stenodontes chevrolati
species.intro: Stenodontes chevrolati is a large prionine longhorn native to southern Florida and parts of the Caribbean. I used to see it only rarely in collections. Captive breeding has made it easier to obtain, and I find it fairly straightforward to rear once I have an active pair. The step I pay closest attention to is separating the young larvae as soon as they hatch.

facts.title: Larval period
facts.text: Usually 1–3 years overall. About 8 months on kinshi in my fastest cultures.

sections.title: Pairing the adults
sections.text: I have never seen my adults feed. They appear to live on reserves accumulated as larvae, and some of mine have lived as long as four months. Once both beetles are active, I introduce the male to the female and watch for mating. My pairs usually mate almost immediately. One mating seems sufficient for the female to lay fertile eggs for the rest of her life. I remove the male afterward because he will keep trying to mate while she is trying to lay.

sections.title: Egg laying and the first galleries
sections.text: For one mated female, I pack raw hardwood sawdust into a container of at least 32 US fl oz (about 0.95 L) and lay a paper towel over the surface. She deposits her eggs on or just below the surface of the sawdust. I expect them to hatch in about a month. The first sign I look for is a set of tiny galleries against the container wall. As soon as I see them, I take the laying box apart and gently sift through the sawdust. I move each hatchling to its own container because the larvae readily cannibalize one another.

sections.title: Choosing a larval substrate
sections.text: I rear each larva in at least 32 fl oz of substrate and prefer a one-gallon jar (3.8 L). I use raw hardwood sawdust, lightly fermented sawdust that has gone through one fermentation, or kinshi, which is sawdust colonized by fungal mycelium. My larvae grew fastest on kinshi, followed by lightly fermented sawdust. On raw sawdust they took about 18–24 months to mature. On kinshi they could reach the same stage in about eight months.

sections.title: Changing food and recognizing pupation
sections.text: With kinshi, I look through the sides of the bottle. When I can no longer see fungus-colonized substrate at the wall, I move the larva to a fresh bottle. With raw or lightly fermented sawdust, I can usually leave the jar for six to eight months between changes. A full-grown larva builds a pupal cell and may spend several months inside. The pupal stage itself lasts about a month. I leave the cell intact and wait for the new adults to become active before introducing another pair.

sections.title: Male size in my collection · Junkai Wang
sections.text: The male I photographed in February 2024 measured about 75 mm. My largest male measured 78 mm. I have kept this species alongside Mallodon dasystomus, another prionine I breed. Even an average male Mallodon can look small when the two are side by side.

species.name: Dynastes grantii
species.intro: Western Hercules beetles appear at lights in the southwestern United States from late summer into autumn. Adults have been observed feeding at velvet ash by day, while grubs have been found in rotten sycamore. When planning a brood, I would set aside a second laying box before introducing the adults. Eggs can take months to hatch, and the female can keep laying while her first clutch develops.

sections.title: Pairing and preparing the laying box
sections.text: J. Kim used one male with one or two females in a container deep enough for 15–25 cm (6–10 in) of premoistened substrate. Adults took beetle jelly or ripe banana. Wild-caught adults often paired promptly, whereas newly emerged captive beetles sometimes needed more time. After seeing two or three matings, Kim removed the male so the female could burrow and lay without further disturbance.

sections.title: Waiting for eggs to hatch
sections.text: Kim’s eggs took anywhere from about two weeks to three months to hatch. To protect a clutch, I would lift the female out when she surfaces and leave the eggs where she laid them. The substrate should stay moist throughout incubation. Date each box when the female goes in and when she comes out. I would count eggs and surviving grubs separately. One of Alan’s females produced 87 eggs. In a separate box holding more than 80 eggs, he eventually recovered 12 living grubs. With a long incubation, I keep each laying box labeled even after moving the adults on.

sections.title: Larval development and adult longevity
sections.text:
The grubs pass through three instars before making a pupal chamber. In one of Alan’s broods a larva reached the prepupal stage well ahead of its siblings. In a display enclosure, cell building was visible on September 23 and a pupa was visible on October 17. When a cell lies against the wall, I would leave it intact and follow the beetle through the side of the enclosure. Kim reported about 12–15 months from egg to adult in his setup.
Adult longevity also varies. Krell and Krell followed a male collected at Arizona’s Southwestern Research Station on August 20, 2014. Kept at room temperature with bark and wood chips, it ate fresh apple about every four days and remained active through winter. It survived nine months and one week after collection, unusually long beside the two to four months commonly reported for the species.

species.name: Euphoria monticola
species.intro: I started my Euphoria monticola culture with several grubs I found beneath decomposing leaves in Arizona. They are difficult to find in the wild. The adults fly in the canopy and visit sap flows, so they can be easy to miss from the ground. I raised my larvae to adults and obtained one captive generation. I rate the species 6 out of 10 for difficulty.

facts.title: Adult feeding in our collection
facts.text: Offer beetle jelly every five days, or apple or banana.

sections.title: Adults and egg laying
sections.text: These southwestern flower chafers occur in Arizona and New Mexico and range south into Mexico. Adults measure about 10–15 mm. The two beetles pictured here give a sense of the color variation, one metallic green and the other blue-black. Mine readily accepted fruit and beetle jelly and lived about one to three months. I recommend a breeding container that holds at least 1.75 US gallons (6.6 L). Offer the adult food at the surface and give females flake soil or an organic substrate of decaying hardwood and well-decomposed leaves in which to lay. They can produce 30 or more eggs.

sections.title: Feeding the larvae
sections.text: The hatchlings can start feeding in the same material their mother laid in. I allow about 18 months for the larval stage, so keep enough of the same food on hand for substrate changes. I lost the next generation after moving the young grubs to potting soil. I can’t say exactly what caused the loss. For another brood I’d keep the grubs on flake soil or replenish the mixture of decayed wood and leaves that supported them earlier.

sections.title: Autumn cocoons and spring emergence
sections.text: The hardest part for me was getting the mature larvae through winter. All of them built cocoons in autumn, then spent several months inside as larvae. Only after I moved the cocoons into a cold garage for winter did the larvae become prepupae. They pupated when the weather warmed in spring, and adults appeared within about a month. I have no measured garage temperature to recommend, and the length of pupation and dormancy varies. If you are following a brood of your own, note when a cell first appears and leave it in place. The larva may spend a season inside before it actually pupates.

species.name: Osmoderma eremicola
species.intro: I give this eastern hermit beetle about two years, sometimes longer, to finish its larval development. Even the second-instar grubs can make chambers and stay inside for weeks. Mine came back out to feed, then molted again before their final winter rest. Despite the long life cycle, I rate the species 3 out of 10 for difficulty.

facts.title: Adult feeding in our collection
facts.text: Offer beetle jelly every five days, or apple or banana.

sections.title: Adults and breeding substrate
sections.text: Adults measure roughly 25–30 mm and live for about one to three months. They fly in the canopy and visit sap flows in the wild. I recommend a breeding container of at least 1.75 US gallons (6.6 L). In captivity I offer fruit or beetle jelly when they become active. Even unfed females laid eggs for me, but they lived for less time and produced fewer eggs than females with access to food. Egg counts can reach 30 or more. To select a pair, look at the head and the plate directly behind it, the pronotum. Steffek and colleagues used the conspicuous depressions in both structures to recognize males.

sections.title: Feeding grubs and temporary chambers
sections.text: The grubs live in pockets of decayed hardwood inside tree cavities. One Wisconsin beetle was reared from rotting silver maple. I use flake soil, decayed wood, or a mixture with thoroughly decomposed hardwood leaves. Once the grubs have reduced their food to a pile of frass, give them fresh substrate. In summer or autumn my second instars made small chambers and remained inside for several weeks, sometimes a month. Leave these chambers alone. The grubs came back out, resumed feeding and quickly reached the third instar. They overwintered as third instars and reached full size by the end of the following year.

sections.title: Overwintering mature larvae
sections.text: Once my third instars were fully grown, I moved them into a garage for about three months. Winter temperatures there were in the low 50s °F (roughly 10–12 °C). A friend also had adults emerge together after keeping the larvae in the mid-60s °F (about 18 °C). Overlapping emergence matters because the adults are relatively short-lived. The pupal stage lasts about a month, and the dormancy period is roughly three weeks. I leave each cell supported by its surrounding substrate. The wall can break simply from lifting it. When the adults emerge, move them into a fresh breeding bin and provide food for the next pairing.

species.name: Chrysina gloriosa
species.intro: I set up my glorious jewel scarabs for breeding as soon as I have active adults. Their one to three months above ground leave little time to spare. Getting eggs is only the beginning. I rate this species 8 out of 10 for difficulty because maintaining it through successive generations has proved much harder.

facts.title: Range
facts.text: Arizona, New Mexico and western Texas

sections.title: Sexing and feeding a pair
sections.text: My adults measure about 20–30 mm. Males tend to be smaller, but I check the underside of the abdomen when choosing a pair. In a female, the last abdominal segment has a pointed, V-shaped outline. In a male, it is more rounded or U-shaped, with a narrow slit visible at the tip. I provide juniper cuttings in a breeding bin of at least 1.75 US gallons (6.6 L). Eastern red cedar (Juniperus virginiana) works well. I change the cuttings every three days and keep old foliage out of the bin. My adults have been prone to fungal and bacterial problems when cuttings are left to deteriorate.

sections.title: Recognizing the laying cycle
sections.text: I leave the eggs where the female lays them. A female typically spends several days feeding on the juniper, burrows for about a day, then comes up to feed again. This cycle can repeat several times. I keep the foliage fresh even when the beetles are below ground. I expect roughly 20–60 eggs, sometimes more. My adults have left the eggs alone, and the grubs can hatch directly into the shared substrate.

sections.title: Feeding the grubs
sections.text: I use regular flake soil and have raised larvae on it through to adulthood. The adult food plant is a poor guide to the grub’s diet. Field workers in southeastern Arizona found larvae in decaying Arizona sycamore (Platanus wrightii), and J. Kim reared them on rotten oak. My larvae generally reach the latter part of their third and final instar by autumn. I allow 1½–3 years for the larval stage and about a month for the pupa.

sections.title: Overwintering and pairing the next generation
sections.text: I keep late third instars cool through the winter, from the low 40s into the 50s °F (roughly 5–15 °C). When I skipped winter cooling, larvae often failed to pupate, or adults emerged so far apart that I could not pair them. I warm the containers in spring and wait. The adults come to the surface on their own after a few months. I keep a newly surfaced female away from males for the first several days and give her fresh juniper to feed on. Persistent mating attempts at this vulnerable stage can kill her.

species.name: Osmoderma subplanatum
species.intro: For young Osmoderma subplanatum I recommend starting with flake soil. Alan’s grubs reached the third instar about a month after he first saw them as first instars. That early growth is encouraging, but leave room in the rearing schedule for a much longer final instar.

facts.title: First to third instar
facts.text: About one month from first to third instar

sections.title: Substrate for growing larvae
sections.text: Alan’s brood completed its first two molts on commercially prepared flake soil. For an alternative larval food, choose well-decayed hardwood. Brett Ratcliffe found about 45 third instars together inside one decayed standing ash in Lincoln, Nebraska. Other Nebraska larvae came from rotting maple and boxelder. Ash can therefore support a brood where decay has softened the wood, and suitable material also occurs in other hardwood trees.

sections.title: From third instar to adult
sections.text: Ratcliffe reared larvae collected in July on pieces of wood from their original ash. He kept them at 27 ± 2 °C in a chamber humidified by evaporation from open water containers. The following February he recovered two pupae and four adults. By June, four individuals were still larvae and many had died. I mention the temperature because it puts those dates in context. Survival was poor in that trial, so I’d use the wood choice and the range of developmental times as guides rather than treating that temperature as optimal.

sections.title: Recognizing and documenting the stages
sections.text: Ratcliffe’s pupae measured 30–36 mm long. They were pale at first and darkened to brown as adult emergence approached. I recommend keeping the collection locality and brood identity on the container through emergence. The third instars of this beetle and Osmoderma eremicola look very much alike, with substantial overlap even in the fine characters of the head. Rearing the Nebraska beetles to adults let Ratcliffe confirm the identification. If you look up his original account, you will find it under the earlier spelling Osmoderma subplanata.

species.name: Osmoderma scabrum
species.intro: For rough hermit beetle larvae, I recommend decayed hardwood with some of its original texture. A grub feeds on the wood, then binds pieces together to make a chamber in which it can spend the winter. Alan’s beetles were in their cells in January.

facts.title: Adult feeding in our collection
facts.text: Offer beetle jelly every five days, or apple or banana.

sections.title: Larval food and cell construction
sections.text: William Saunders found large white grubs with reddish heads feeding inside decaying apple and cherry wood. Even a tree that still bears leaves can have a soft pocket of rot inside. For the enclosure, choose wood decayed enough for the grubs to eat, and leave some of its original texture for the mature larvae to build with. Saunders described them gathering bits of wood in autumn and cementing the pieces into an oval cell. When you change the substrate late in the season, look for these structures before crumbling an apparently solid lump.

sections.title: Winter observations
sections.text: If you uncover a cell, keep the wall and the wood that supports it together. A larva can still be inside after it finishes building. I recommend recording the date you first see the cell and the date the adult comes to the surface separately. In Alan’s culture, individuals were resting in their cells on January 24, 2026. In Saunders’s field observations, grubs built cells in autumn and adults appeared the following summer. A substantial part of the winter interval can therefore pass before an adult is ready to emerge.

sections.title: Adult activity and pairing
sections.text: Saunders observed adults in July. They sheltered by day and fed on sap after dark, so evening is a good time to look for an active beetle at the surface. Adults have coarsely sculptured wing covers, which distinguish them from the smoother Osmoderma eremicola. To select a pair, wait until the beetles surface. Steffek and colleagues distinguished males by the conspicuous depressions on the head and pronotum, the plate immediately behind the head. If you consult older accounts of the rough hermit beetle, look for the spelling Osmoderma scabra.

species.name: Lucanus mazama
species.intro: I had good emergence in my cottonwood stag beetles, with a number of adults coming out together. The newly emerged adults were dark and fairly understated, but seeing a whole group mature together was one of my favorite parts of keeping them. For breeding, flake soil works as a laying substrate. For the larvae, decaying oak offers a second, particularly well documented option.

facts.title: Adult feeding in our collection
facts.text: Offer beetle jelly every five days, or apple or banana.

sections.title: Pairing and egg laying
sections.text: Choose an active male and female. The male’s short, inward-curving mandibles are noticeably larger than the female’s. In Colorado adults are most often seen from mid-July to mid-August, sometimes at lights. Prepare the laying box with flake soil before introducing the pair. Captive beetles have reproduced on it, and IB Exotic notes that females can start depositing eggs directly into substrate within a week of mating. You can set up a pair this way even if you have no intact rotten log.

sections.title: Sorting and feeding the brood
sections.text: Have containers ready when you open the laying box. Alan recovered 46 larvae from one enclosure, enough to make an unplanned transfer quite a job. To raise grubs on wood, Reyes-Castillo and colleagues reared third instars from a decaying oak stump in Chihuahua. They supplied plenty of decaying oak and gumbo-limbo wood and debris. At an average of 23.3 °C and 80% relative humidity, the grubs stayed buried and fed in the woody material. Of 16 larvae, nine pupated and seven reached adulthood.

sections.title: Pupation and adult activity
sections.text: Leave a layer of woody debris in place as the larvae mature. In the Mexican group they pupated in this debris, apparently without building a cocoon. Five prepupae took five to eight days to become pupae, and seven pupae molted into adults after a further 31–35 days. Newly formed beetles can remain out of sight beneath a log. The captive adults in this study spent much of their time there and fed infrequently, with some surviving up to 18 months. IB Exotic gives approximately one year for the complete cycle in its breeding account.

species.name: Lucanus capreolus
species.intro: For a reddish-brown stag beetle laying box, I recommend setting pieces of rotten hardwood into fine fermented wood substrate. The material touching each piece is worth a close look when you sort the brood. A female can leave eggs tucked right against the wood, with food already within reach of the hatchlings.

facts.title: Adult feeding in our collection
facts.text: Offer beetle jelly every five days, or apple or banana.

sections.title: Preparing the pair and laying box
sections.text: Look for the pale and dark areas on the femora when confirming the adults’ identity. The similar smooth stag beetle, Lucanus placidus, has uniformly dark femora. I often see fungal growth on wild reddish-brown stags, so I look over each adult when selecting a pair. Wild adults visit sap, and captive adults will drink diluted maple syrup or sugar water. Give a laying female access to both the wood and surrounding substrate. Benjamin Harink describes eggs beside rotten wood in fine material including fermented sawdust. Eggs have also been found in the decaying wood itself, so keep occupied pieces intact while checking the loose material.

sections.title: Housing and feeding larvae
sections.text: Set up cups before taking down a productive box. Alan found young grubs in August 2025 and recovered 65 larvae when he took down a September breeding enclosure. For a brood that size, I recommend the individual setup that Leg & Leaf uses with captive-bred grubs. Fill a 16 fl oz cup with lightly packed, damp flake soil or decayed hardwood for a younger grub. Move a third instar into at least 24 fl oz. Check the food every two to three months. When fecal pellets accumulate on the surface, replenish the feeding substrate.

sections.title: Development and dormancy
sections.text: Expect the largest change in your timetable at the third instar. Leg & Leaf gives about a month for the first instar, one to two months for the second and 10–22 months for the third. The head capsule enlarges with each molt. Mature larvae can pupate in soil beside the feeding wood. Allow one to two months for the pupa, then four to six months of adult dormancy in Leg & Leaf’s stock. Wait until the beetles become active before pairing them. Alan obtained adults in September and later encountered abdominal abnormalities in some freshly emerged beetles. He could not identify a cause.

species.name: Lucanus placidus
species.intro: I recovered 54 larvae from a single smooth stag beetle female. With a brood that size, I like to have the next set of cups ready before I open the laying box. The long wait comes later, when the grubs finish feeding and start shaping their individual pupal cells.

facts.title: Adult feeding in our collection
facts.text: Offer beetle jelly every five days, or apple or banana.

sections.title: Adults and activity
sections.text: I see these beetles fly readily in May. Check for adult activity after dusk. Wild adults dig burrows several inches deep and can spend the day out of sight, with males sometimes meeting and fighting on open ground. Both sexes resemble the reddish-brown stag beetle, Lucanus capreolus. In the smooth stag the femora are uniformly dark, and the inner edge of a male’s mandible usually carries several teeth. Butterfly Wings N’ Wishes feeds its captive adults banana, watermelon or beetle jelly. Field observations suggest that females may lay eggs in sod, with grubs feeding underground near stumps or roots.

sections.title: Feeding individual grubs
sections.text: For older larvae, I recommend starting with the birch-based setup used by Butterfly Wings N’ Wishes. House one grub in a 16 fl oz cup with flake soil and decaying hardwood, keep the substrate slightly damp and hold at 18–22 °C. Watch how the feeding layer changes. Crumbly wood gradually gives way to dark, flattened pellets. When pellets occupy most of the cup, mix fresh, soft decayed hardwood through the feeding layer. The facility estimates eight to ten months for the larval period under those conditions.

sections.title: Pupal cells and emergence
sections.text: A mature larva may work its body rhythmically against the substrate to form an oval chamber near the bottom of the cup. Stop mixing the substrate at this stage. On July 26 Alan found that all his previously stalled larvae had become prepupae after a faulty air conditioner cooled the room for several days. By July 31 he had a pupa. The room temperature was not measured, so I would let an undisturbed chamber develop at the usual rearing temperature. A. A. Girault tracked one nearly grown grub from a Virginia stump through the full transition. It became a prepupa around August 1, pupated on August 3 and reached the adult molt on October 6. Give the intact cell time even if several weeks pass with little visible change.

species.name: Dorcus parallelus
species.intro: For breeding the antelope stag beetle, I recommend putting decaying hardwood into the laying box in pieces large enough to keep their shape. A female can lay inside wood that still feels fairly solid. Once the larvae are feeding, prepared flake soil gives you a way to rear them on fermented hardwood sawdust.

facts.title: Adult feeding in our collection
facts.text: Offer beetle jelly every five days, or apple or banana.

sections.title: Choosing a pair
sections.text: Start by checking both adults from above. Dorcus parallelus and Dorcus brevis overlap in parts of eastern North America, and a small male can have surprisingly short jaws. Look at the rear corners of the pronotum, the shield immediately behind the head. In D. parallelus the corners sit well forward of the wing covers. In D. brevis they come close to the wing covers. M. J. Paulsen also illustrates a dense patch of hairs on the inner face of each hind tibia in male D. parallelus.

sections.title: Setting up the laying box
sections.text: Oak, maple and linden are all recorded breeding woods. Choose pieces at different stages of decay and pack partly fermented wood substrate around them. My reason for offering a choice is that females have used wood of different consistencies in captivity. Steven of Beetle-Experience found his eggs inside the firmer pieces of rotten log. KevinD also lists soft, white-rotted wood and compacted substrate for this species. When inspecting the box, lift each piece with the material against it still in place. Set any wood that may hold eggs back in the enclosure. A piece can look intact from the outside even when a female has laid inside it.

sections.title: Rearing the grubs
sections.text: For a growing grub I recommend prepared flake soil or the decaying hardwood it is already feeding in. If a grub is exposed when you lift a log, retain some of its feeding wood when transferring it. Alan saw a larva in his breeding enclosure in September 2025. In May 2026 he counted five surviving grubs in one culture, and his June setup used flake soil prepared to @doctorderange’s recipe. The Bull Run Mountains Natural Area Preserve puts the larval feeding period at roughly one to two years in nature. Plan for a long supply of decaying hardwood and leave a mature grub’s pupal chamber intact when checking its container.

substrate.credit: Flour ratio correction by Leg and Leaf: 15 lb of unbleached flour per 40 lb of sawdust. The original 20 lb batch therefore uses 7.5 lb of flour.

sections.title: Beetle Substrate Guide
sections.subtitle: Lets make this as easy as possible
paragraphs: Here are the very basics: in regards to US native species, Dynastes tityus and granti, Strategus aloeus and antaeus, Gymnetis thula and any Cotinis species, Osmoderma species and Euphoria species can be raised on "Organic Raised Bed Soil" alone! If a larger size is desired, simply mix in raw sawdust! This will be explained in the next slide. But without any mixtures, the organic soil alone will achieve average sized adult beetles!

sections.title: Mixing the Organic Raised Bed Soil
sections.subtitle: Say goodbye to hard to make flake soil!
paragraphs: So if you decide to go down the dark path of ditching flake soil once and for all, but still want that sweet large major male, know that it is still very doable, and easy! Mix in 3/10th of the substrate mass in raw sawdust, you can use any of the hardwood grilling pellets consisting of Oak or Mesquite wood. I personally opt for Mesquite as it is the most affordable option. Make sure the sawdust expands and stir it with the "Organic Raised Bed Soil" throughly. Leave the mixture for two weeks, and stir it whenever you remember to do so (doesn't have to be often). Once the two weeks is up, it is ready for you to add beetles!

A. make sure the organic soil you use do not compose of cow manure. Cow manure contains a bacteria that can cause leg rot with a lot of beetle larvae species and can kill your larvae quickly. That said, most "Organic Raised Bed Soil" purchased from Walmart or Home Depot does not contain cow manure and can be used without issues.
B. This substrate mix is not meant for: any US Lucanid (stag beetles), and any of them Phileurus or Hemiphileurus species.
C. If the intent is to raise large cetoniids (flower beetles), adding a large portion of rotting leaves will also yield desirable results, although raw sawdust works perfectly fine.

sections.title: Making Flake Soil
sections.subtitle: You gotta do it sometime
paragraphs: You really don't have to stress about making flake soil - things ferment in the wild all without human intervention after all. But sometimes, we just gotta speed it up!

sections.title: How to Make Flake Soil
sections.subtitle: Can't be that hard can it?
paragraphs: First up - if you leave raw sawdust by itself in a moist state long enough, certain lucanids will eat it. Yes, you heard me right, the more hardy species will do just fine on aged sawdust. But this might cost you 6 months - a year's time.
So, how do you make flake soil?

Well, you will need ingredients first. 20lbs of hardwood grilling pellets of just about any brand will do the trick for the wood part, but oak and mesquite are your best choices. Then, you need to add 7.5lbs of unbleached flour, and some dry yeast.
The first step is to pour out and expand the pellets with water, and then turn it into sawdust. Warm water works best with this step, but cold will do just fine.

Then you pour the flour into the expanded pellets, along with a table spoon of yeast. You want to mix throughly here, so there isn't huge clumps of flour - an occasional small piece here and there is fine.

The end result should be damp, but not wet. You can check it by squeezing the substrate. It should form a clump and not fall apart when released, all the while having no water come out. If you made it too wet, leave it in somewhere sunny for a few days and stir more often, you will be fine.

Now the waiting game begins. In this stage, you want to mix up the substrate at least once in 2 days (once a day is better). You should notice the substrate heating up, if it does not heat up, simply add more yeast.
It will be about 3 weeks to a month before the soil is ready. Be sure to wait till the substrate is fully cooled down.
Yay, now you have flake soil! The rest of beetle keeping will be a breeze!
